title: HTTP & HTTPS
summary: The protocol powering every webpage. Understand requests, responses, methods, status codes, headers, cookies, and how HTTPS adds encryption — plus where HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 make it faster.

blocks.markdown:
**HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol)** is the application-layer protocol browsers and servers use to exchange data.

- A **client** (browser) sends a **request**; the **server** replies with a **response**.
- HTTP is **stateless** — each request is independent; the server remembers nothing between them.
- **HTTPS** wraps HTTP in **TLS**, adding encryption and authentication.
- HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 are successors that improve speed and efficiency.

See [application-layer-protocols](application-layer-protocols).

blocks.subTitle: At a glance
blocks.markdown:
Key terms in one pass.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Stateless | Server forgets each request after replying |
| TLS | Cryptographic layer that HTTPS runs on |
| Idempotent | Repeating the call has the same effect as one call |

**Stateless** = simpler servers, but sessions need workarounds (cookies).

Every HTTP exchange has the same shape.

- **Request:** method + URL + headers + optional body. Sent by the client.
- **Response:** status line + headers + optional body. Sent by the server.
- HTTP is **stateless**: each request carries all the context it needs; the server holds no memory of prior requests from the same client.

Stateless design keeps servers simple and horizontally scalable — any server can handle any request.

blocks.subTitle: Raw example
blocks.markdown:
A minimal HTTP/1.1 request and its response.

```http
GET /users/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Accept: application/json

```

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 27

{"id":42,"name":"Alice"}
```

The blank line separates headers from the body. The request body is empty for GET.

Methods tell the server **what to do** with the resource.

| Method | Action | Idempotent? |
|---|---|---|
| GET | Read a resource | Yes |
| POST | Create / trigger | No |
| PUT | Replace entirely | Yes |
| PATCH | Partial update | No |
| DELETE | Remove | Yes |

**Idempotent**: repeating it N times = same result as once. GET, PUT, DELETE are safe to retry. POST is not.

blocks.subTitle: The five families
blocks.markdown:
Every response carries a 3-digit status code. The first digit is the family.

- **1xx Informational** — request received, still processing (rare to see directly).
- **2xx Success** — request succeeded. `200 OK`, `201 Created`.
- **3xx Redirection** — client must follow a new URL. `301 Moved Permanently`, `302 Found`.
- **4xx Client error** — client did something wrong. `400`, `401`, `403`, `404`.
- **5xx Server error** — server failed. `500 Internal Server Error`, `503 Service Unavailable`.

blocks.subTitle: Common ones to know
blocks.markdown:
The codes every developer hits.

| Code | Name | Means |
|---|---|---|
| 200 | OK | Success, body returned |
| 301 | Moved Permanently | Resource lives at new URL forever |
| 401 | Unauthorized | No valid credentials supplied |
| 403 | Forbidden | Credentials valid but access denied |
| 404 | Not Found | Resource doesn't exist |
| 500 | Internal Server Error | Bug/crash on the server |

401 vs 403: **401** = not logged in; **403** = logged in but not allowed.

**Headers** are key-value metadata sent with every request and response.

- **Request headers:** `Host` (target server), `Accept` (expected content types), `Authorization` (credentials), `Cookie` (session token).
- **Response headers:** `Content-Type` (MIME type of body, e.g. `application/json`), `Set-Cookie` (create a cookie on client), `Cache-Control` (caching rules), `Location` (redirect target).

`Content-Type` is the most-missed source of 415/parsing errors — always match it to the actual body format.

HTTP is stateless, so **cookies** are the main workaround for recognising returning users.

1. Server sends `Set-Cookie: session=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure` in the response.
2. Browser stores it and includes `Cookie: session=abc123` in every future request to that domain.
3. Server looks up `abc123` in a **session store** to find the user's state.

**HttpOnly** blocks JS from reading the cookie (XSS defence). **Secure** sends it only over HTTPS.

**HTTPS** = HTTP running over **TLS (Transport Layer Security)**.

TLS adds three things HTTP alone cannot provide:
- **Encryption** — payload is unreadable to anyone in between (no eavesdropping).
- **Integrity** — tampering with data in transit is detected.
- **Authentication** — the server presents a **certificate** signed by a trusted CA, so the client knows it's talking to the real site.

See [tls-ssl](tls-ssl) for the full handshake. Port 443 = HTTPS; port 80 = HTTP.

blocks.subTitle: 1.1 vs 2 vs 3
blocks.markdown:
Three versions, each solving the previous one's bottleneck.

| Version | Transport | Key improvement |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP/1.1 | TCP | Persistent connections (keep-alive) |
| HTTP/2 | TCP | Multiplexing, binary framing |
| HTTP/3 | QUIC (UDP) | No head-of-line blocking at transport |

**Keep-alive**: reuse one TCP connection for many requests instead of reconnecting each time.

blocks.subTitle: HTTP/1.1
blocks.markdown:
**HTTP/1.1** (1997) is still the baseline.

- **Persistent connections (keep-alive)**: one TCP socket reused across multiple requests — avoids the overhead of a new handshake each time.
- **Head-of-line (HOL) blocking**: requests on one connection are processed in order; a slow response blocks everything behind it.
- Workaround: browsers open 6–8 parallel TCP connections per domain, which wastes resources.

blocks.subTitle: HTTP/2
blocks.markdown:
**HTTP/2** (2015) fixes HOL blocking at the HTTP layer.

- **Multiplexing**: multiple requests and responses flow concurrently on **one TCP connection** as independent **streams** — no waiting in line.
- **Binary framing**: data is split into binary frames instead of plain text, making parsing faster.
- **Header compression (HPACK)**: repeated headers are compressed, reducing overhead on every request.

Downside: a single TCP packet loss still stalls all streams (TCP-level HOL blocking remains).

blocks.subTitle: HTTP/3
blocks.markdown:
**HTTP/3** runs on **QUIC** instead of TCP.

- **QUIC** is a transport protocol built on UDP, with reliability and congestion control built in.
- Packet loss only stalls the **stream** it belongs to — other streams keep flowing. TCP HOL blocking is gone.
- Built-in TLS 1.3: the first packet establishes security, cutting connection setup by one round-trip.

See [quic-http3](quic-http3). HTTP/3 is the protocol of choice for latency-sensitive apps.

Common mistakes:

- **"GET can have a body."** Technically allowed, but proxies and servers often strip it — don't.
- **"401 and 403 are the same."** 401 = missing/invalid credentials; 403 = valid credentials, but access denied.
- **"HTTPS hides the domain."** The domain appears in SNI during the TLS handshake — it's visible to network observers.
- **"HTTP/2 fixes all HOL blocking."** It fixes it at the HTTP layer; TCP packet loss still stalls all streams.

blocks.subTitle: GET vs POST
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between GET and POST?**

**GET** retrieves a resource; parameters go in the URL; it is **idempotent** and safe to cache. **POST** submits data in the request body to create or trigger something; it is **not idempotent** and must not be cached blindly.

Key rule: never use GET to change server state — caches and proxies will replay it.

blocks.subTitle: Stateless & cookies
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Is HTTP stateless? How do cookies help?**

Yes — each request carries no memory of previous ones. Cookies work around this: the server sets a token (`Set-Cookie`) on login; the browser echoes it (`Cookie`) on every request; the server resolves the token to a session in a store.

The protocol stays stateless; the session illusion lives in that store, not in HTTP itself.

blocks.subTitle: Status code meanings
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What do 301, 401, 403, 404, and 500 mean?**

- **301** — resource moved permanently; client should update its bookmark.
- **401** — unauthenticated; send credentials.
- **403** — authenticated but forbidden; no amount of credentials helps.
- **404** — resource not found at this URL.
- **500** — server crashed; nothing the client can do.

Interviewers often probe 401 vs 403 — they are not synonyms.

blocks.subTitle: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What did HTTP/2 improve over HTTP/1.1?**

**HTTP/1.1** processes requests in order on a connection — a slow response blocks the rest (HOL blocking). It workarounds this with multiple parallel TCP connections per domain.

**HTTP/2** multiplexes all requests on a single TCP connection as independent streams — no ordering, no blocking at the HTTP layer. Binary framing and header compression further cut overhead.

blocks.subTitle: What HTTPS adds
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What does HTTPS add over plain HTTP?**

HTTPS = HTTP + TLS. TLS provides three guarantees HTTP cannot:
1. **Encryption** — body and headers are unreadable in transit.
2. **Integrity** — any tampering is detected and the connection fails.
3. **Server authentication** — the certificate proves which server you're talking to.

Without HTTPS, an attacker on the network can read passwords and inject content.

blocks.subTitle: Idempotency
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is an idempotent HTTP method and why does it matter?**

An **idempotent** method produces the same server state no matter how many times it is called with the same input. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not.

It matters for **retries**: if a network timeout leaves you unsure whether the call landed, you can safely retry an idempotent method — retrying POST may create duplicates.
